Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The European Union will launch its first naval operation Tuesday, protecting vessels from pirate attacks off the coast of Somalia, EU policy chief Javier Solana announced Monday. A French army helicopter taking off from French frigate Nivose,  on patrol in the Gulf of Aden. EU foreign ministers approved the mission during their regular meeting in Brussels on Monday. Solana said the operation is "very important" because EU vessels will be operating "in a place in the world that everybody's looking at because of the new problems related to piracy." "It's very important that we have taken that decision to launch it tomorrow," he added. The EU naval force will take over the role of escorting United Nations World Food Program vessels carrying food and relief supplies to war-torn Somalia, an EU news release said. Its mandate, which is spelled out in several U.N. Security Council resolutions, also will include "the protection of vulnerable vessels cruising off the Somali coast, and the deterrence, prevention and repression of acts of piracy and armed robbery off the Somali coast," the news release stated. The deployment follows a decision by the European Council in September that established a coordination cell that supported surveillance and protection operations by several member states off the Somali coast. Piracy has become increasingly common in that area this year, particularly in the Gulf of Aden. So far, pirates have attacked almost 100 vessels off Somalia's coast and successfully hijacked nearly 40, according to the International Maritime Bureau. Those hijacked vessels include an enormous oil tanker, a chemical tanker, and a ship laden with Soviet-era arms, including tanks. The pirates normally hold the ships for ransom. The Somali-based pirates have extended their reach beyond Somalia's coastline. On Saturday, a Dutch-operated container ship outran pirates off the coast of Tanzania, an IMB official told CNN. A luxury cruise ship carrying more than 1,000 passengers and crew successfully outran pirates off the coast of Yemen last weekend. A multinational fleet -- including vessels from the United States, NATO member states, Russia and India -- has been patrolling the Indian Ocean waters near the Gulf of Aden, which connects the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. Around 20,000 oil tankers, freighters and merchant vessels pass along the crucial shipping route each year. In a recent interview provided to CNN, a pirate leader claimed attacks on shipping would continue so long as life in Somalia remained desperate. "The pirates are living between life and death," said the pirate leader, identified by only one name, Boyah. "Who can stop them? Americans and British all put together cannot do anything."

(CNN) — EU foreign policy chief Javier Solana said Monday that the European Union would begin its first naval mission on Tuesday to defend ships against pirate attacks near Somalia.

A French military helicopter was seen lifting off from the French frigate *Nivose* while the vessel patrolled the Gulf of Aden.

The operation was authorized by EU foreign ministers at their regular Monday meeting in Brussels. Solana described the mission as highly significant, noting that European ships would be deployed in a part of the world receiving intense international attention because of the growing piracy threat. He also emphasized the importance of the decision to start the mission the following day.

According to an EU statement, the European naval force will assume responsibility for escorting United Nations World Food Program ships transporting food and humanitarian assistance to conflict-ravaged Somalia. Its authority, established through several U.N. Security Council resolutions, also covers safeguarding at-risk ships traveling off Somalia, as well as discouraging, preventing and suppressing piracy and armed robbery in those waters.

The deployment stems from a European Council decision in September to create a coordination unit supporting surveillance and protection efforts conducted by several EU member countries near the Somali coast.

Pirate activity has risen sharply in the region this year, especially in the Gulf of Aden. International Maritime Bureau figures show that nearly 100 ships have been attacked off Somalia, with close to 40 successfully seized. Captured vessels include a massive oil tanker, a chemical tanker and a ship carrying Soviet-era weapons, among them tanks. Pirates typically demand ransom in exchange for releasing the ships.

Somalia-based pirate groups have also begun operating farther from the country’s shores. An IMB official told CNN that a Dutch-operated container vessel escaped pursuing pirates near Tanzania on Saturday. The previous weekend, a luxury cruise liner carrying more than 1,000 passengers and crew also managed to outrun pirates off Yemen.

Warships from a multinational force—including vessels belonging to the United States, NATO countries, Russia and India—have been monitoring Indian Ocean waters around the Gulf of Aden, the passage linking the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea. Approximately 20,000 oil tankers, cargo ships and other commercial vessels travel through this strategically important route every year.

In a recent interview made available to CNN, a pirate commander said assaults on ships would persist while conditions in Somalia remained desperate. The leader, identified only as Boyah, said pirates live on the boundary between survival and death and claimed that even the combined power of the Americans and British could not stop them.

The European Union is preparing to launch its first naval operation off the coast of Somalia in an effort to protect humanitarian deliveries and commercial shipping from a sharp rise in piracy.

The mission, operating under a United Nations-backed mandate, will deploy European warships and surveillance aircraft to patrol the Gulf of Aden and waters near Somalia. Its main responsibilities will include escorting vessels chartered by the World Food Program, protecting other vulnerable ships, and helping to deter, prevent and suppress acts of piracy and armed robbery at sea.

World Food Program shipments are especially important because millions of Somalis depend on international food assistance. Much of that aid arrives by sea, making cargo vessels potential targets for pirate groups operating from Somalia’s largely ungoverned coastline. Naval escorts are intended to ensure that relief supplies can reach the country without interruption or excessive risk to crews.

The operation follows a dramatic increase in attacks on shipping. Pirates have carried out nearly 100 attacks this year and successfully hijacked about 40 vessels, often holding ships, cargoes and crews for ransom. Their targets have ranged from small commercial vessels to large tankers, demonstrating an ability to operate farther from shore and across a wider area than in previous years.

European officials say the deployment will complement patrols already conducted by the United States, NATO members and other countries. Warships from several nations have been sent to the region, reflecting growing concern about the security of the Gulf of Aden, one of the world’s busiest maritime routes and a key link between Europe, Asia and the Middle East.

The EU mission also illustrates the difficulty of combating piracy across such a vast stretch of water. Naval forces may be able to escort selected vessels and respond to attacks, but officials acknowledge that ships cannot be protected everywhere at all times. Questions also remain about how suspected pirates should be detained, prosecuted and transferred to national authorities.

Even so, the operation marks a significant step in European security cooperation and the international response to piracy. By protecting humanitarian shipments and increasing the naval presence off Somalia, the EU hopes to make attacks more difficult, safeguard seafarers and preserve vital trade and aid routes as pirate groups continue to expand their reach.

**EU launches first naval mission to fight piracy off Somalia**

**BRUSSELS, Belgium** — The European Union has launched its first naval operation, deploying warships and surveillance aircraft to combat piracy off the coast of Somalia and protect humanitarian aid shipments traveling through one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors.

The mission, known as **Operation Atalanta**, will escort vessels carrying food for the United Nations’ World Food Programme, safeguard vulnerable commercial ships and deter armed groups operating in the Gulf of Aden and the western Indian Ocean.

The operation began in December 2008 amid a sharp rise in attacks on merchant vessels. Somali pirates have seized dozens of ships, taking crews hostage and demanding multimillion-dollar ransoms. The crisis has disrupted traffic near the Suez Canal, a vital route linking Europe and Asia.

EU officials said the multinational force would include warships, maritime patrol aircraft and personnel from several member states. Its headquarters will be at Northwood in Britain.

Naval forces will be authorized to monitor high-risk waters, respond to distress calls and detain suspected pirates in accordance with international law and United Nations resolutions.

Somalia has lacked an effective central government for years, allowing armed groups to operate from coastal communities with limited interference. International officials say piracy cannot be eliminated by naval patrols alone and will also require greater political stability and economic development on land.

Operation Atalanta marks a significant expansion of the EU’s security role and is expected to coordinate with NATO vessels and other international naval forces already patrolling the region.

counterfactuals.output:
# EU ministers approve anti-piracy naval force off Somalia

**BRUSSELS, Nov. 10, 2008 —** European Union foreign ministers approved the bloc’s first naval operation on Monday, authorizing warships and surveillance aircraft to protect humanitarian aid deliveries and commercial shipping from escalating pirate attacks in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia.

The mission, known as **Operation Atalanta**, will escort vessels carrying food for the United Nations World Food Program, patrol high-risk shipping lanes and take action to deter, prevent and repress acts of piracy. It is expected to begin operating in December under British command from a headquarters at Northwood, near London.

EU officials said the force could include as many as six warships and three maritime-patrol aircraft at any one time, although its exact size will depend on contributions from member states. The initial mandate is expected to last one year.

The decision comes amid a surge in hijackings along one of the world’s busiest maritime trade routes. Pirates operating from Somalia’s largely lawless coastline have attacked scores of ships this year, seizing merchant vessels and demanding multimillion-dollar ransoms.

Among the most prominent cases is the September capture of the Ukrainian-operated cargo ship **MV Faina**, which was carrying tanks, ammunition and other military equipment. The vessel and its crew remain held off Somalia. Earlier in the year, pirates seized the French luxury yacht **Le Ponant**, prompting a French military operation that led to the capture of several suspected pirates after the hostages were released.

The attacks have raised shipping costs, forced some companies to consider avoiding the Suez Canal and intensified concern about the safety of aid shipments to Somalia, where millions of people depend on international food assistance.

World Food Program vessels have received military escorts from individual European and allied countries since late 2007. France, Denmark, the Netherlands and Canada have taken turns protecting the shipments, which would otherwise be highly vulnerable while approaching Somali ports. EU officials said Atalanta will place those escorts on a more continuous and coordinated footing.

“The protection of humanitarian deliveries is a central priority,” an EU official said. “At the same time, the operation will help safeguard vulnerable commercial shipping transiting the area.”

The European force will operate alongside a growing collection of international naval patrols. NATO ships have been deployed to escort aid vessels and conduct anti-piracy patrols, while the U.S.-led Combined Task Force 150 maintains a broader maritime-security presence in the region. Russia and India have also sent warships, and other countries have offered escorts or considered deployments.

Coordination will be crucial because the patrol area stretches across hundreds of thousands of square miles. Naval officials have warned that warships cannot protect every merchant vessel and have urged shipping companies to maintain watches, increase speed in dangerous waters and follow recommended transit corridors.

The EU operation will act under international law and U.N. Security Council resolutions permitting foreign forces, with Somalia’s consent, to take action against pirates in Somali territorial waters. Questions remain over where captured suspects would be prosecuted, an issue complicated by differing national laws and evidentiary standards.

European officials said the naval deployment is intended to address the immediate threat at sea, not the conditions driving piracy. Somalia has lacked an effective central government for nearly two decades, and coastal communities have become bases for heavily armed criminal groups using speedboats, satellite phones and captured “mother ships” to extend their reach.

Diplomats acknowledged that lasting progress will require greater stability and economic opportunity on land. But with attacks increasing and humanitarian deliveries at risk, they said an organized naval response could no longer be delayed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the European Union’s response to the surge in Somali piracy, explaining the operation’s mandate, the importance of the shipping route, and examples of recent pirate attacks.
counterfactuals.output:
## European Union response to the resurgence of Somali piracy

The European Union has reinforced **EU Naval Force Somalia – Operation Atalanta**, its long-running counter-piracy mission, following the renewed hijacking of merchant ships in the western Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden from late 2023 onward. The resurgence ended several years in which successful Somali pirate attacks had been rare.

### Operation Atalanta’s mandate

Launched in 2008 and headquartered at Rota, Spain, Atalanta deploys European warships, helicopters and maritime-patrol aircraft. Its current mandate, extended into 2027, includes:

- Deterring, preventing and repressing piracy and armed robbery at sea.
- Protecting vessels carrying World Food Programme aid and other vulnerable shipping.
- Escorting or monitoring merchant vessels transiting high-risk waters.
- Disrupting pirate “mother ships,” which allow gangs to operate hundreds of nautical miles offshore.
- Monitoring illicit maritime activity, including arms and narcotics trafficking and suspicious fishing.
- Supporting regional maritime-security forces and coordinating with independent naval deployments.

Atalanta provides threat assessments and operational coordination through the **Maritime Security Centre – Indian Ocean**. It also works with merchant ships following industry “best management practices,” such as maintaining lookouts, increasing speed, hardening access points and preparing protected citadels.

The operation should not be confused with **EUNAVFOR Aspides**, launched in 2024 to defend commercial shipping from Houthi missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. The two missions operate in connected waters and share information, but Atalanta’s principal focus remains piracy and maritime crime around Somalia and the western Indian Ocean.

### Why the route matters

The waters off Somalia lead into the **Gulf of Aden and Bab el-Mandeb Strait**, connecting the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea, Suez Canal and Mediterranean. This is one of the world’s most important maritime corridors:

- Roughly **12–15% of global trade** and a significant share of container traffic normally pass through the Red Sea–Suez route.
- The corridor carries oil, liquefied natural gas, manufactured goods and food between Asia, Europe and the Middle East.
- Avoiding the area and sailing around the Cape of Good Hope can add approximately **10–14 days**, increasing fuel, crew, insurance and freight costs.

The return of Somali piracy has therefore compounded the disruption caused by Houthi attacks farther north. Somali pirates generally seek ransom by seizing vessels and crews, whereas Houthi forces have used missiles, drones and explosive boats for political and military purposes.

### Examples of the renewed attacks

- **MV Ruen, December 2023:** Pirates seized the Malta-flagged bulk carrier in the Arabian Sea, the first successful hijacking of a major commercial vessel by Somali pirates in years. The ship was later used as a mother ship for further operations. The Indian Navy recaptured it in March 2024 and detained 35 suspected pirates.

- **Lila Norfolk, January 2024:** Armed men boarded the Liberian-flagged bulk carrier in the North Arabian Sea. The crew sheltered in the ship’s citadel, and an Indian naval intervention secured the vessel.

- **MV Abdullah, March 2024:** Somali pirates hijacked the Bangladesh-flagged bulk carrier and its 23 crew while it was carrying coal from Mozambique to the United Arab Emirates. The ship and crew were released in April after negotiations and a reported ransom payment.

- **Basilisk, May 2024:** Pirates boarded the Liberian-flagged merchant ship several hundred nautical miles east of Somalia. The crew entered the citadel, and Spanish forces from Operation Atalanta’s flagship intervened, freed the vessel and treated an injured crew member.

### Assessment

The renewed attacks demonstrated that Somali pirate networks had retained the personnel, coastal support and experience needed to resume long-range operations when naval coverage and merchant vigilance weakened. Instability ashore, economic hardship, illegal-fishing grievances and the diversion of international naval attention toward the Red Sea all contributed to the opportunity.

Atalanta’s response combines patrols and direct interventions with merchant-shipping guidance and international coordination. Although naval action has prevented several seizures, the large operating area means warships cannot escort every vessel. The EU therefore treats continued surveillance, hardened shipboard procedures, regional law-enforcement capacity and prosecution of detained pirates as essential to preventing the resurgence from becoming sustained.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
**EU Naval Force to Begin Anti-Piracy Mission Off Somalia**

*December 8, 2008 — Brussels*

The European Union will begin its first naval operation on Monday, deploying warships and aircraft off Somalia to protect relief shipments and commercial vessels from a sharp rise in pirate attacks.

Operation Atalanta will bring together ships from Britain, France, Germany, Greece, Spain and other EU members. The force will patrol the Gulf of Aden and waters near the Somali coast, escort vessels carrying food for the United Nations World Food Programme and respond to suspected acts of piracy.

EU foreign policy chief Javier Solana called the deployment “a very important step for the European Union,” saying the mission demonstrated Europe’s ability to act jointly beyond its borders. The force, he said, would help “deter, prevent and repress acts of piracy and armed robbery” in one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors.

The operation replaces and expands upon temporary escort arrangements established by individual countries and NATO. It is expected to involve roughly six warships at any one time, supported by maritime patrol aircraft and coordinated from a headquarters in Northwood, England.

Piracy has surged amid nearly two decades of conflict and weak government in Somalia. More than 100 ships have reportedly been attacked in the region this year, with dozens seized for ransom. The November capture of the Saudi-owned supertanker *Sirius Star*, carrying about $100 million worth of crude oil, underscored the pirates’ growing reach.

Abshir Boyah, a prominent pirate leader based in Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland region, defended the attacks as an economic response to lawlessness and foreign exploitation.

“Piracy is our way of earning a living,” Boyah said in remarks reported earlier this year. He has also accused foreign vessels of illegal fishing in Somali waters, an argument frequently used by pirate groups to justify hijackings.

European officials reject such claims, noting that crews from many countries have been held for months under threat of violence. They say Atalanta’s commanders will operate under rules permitting them to intercept, detain and transfer suspected pirates for prosecution where legal arrangements allow.

Solana acknowledged that warships alone could not solve the crisis. “The problem of piracy has its roots on land,” he said, emphasizing that lasting security would depend on restoring effective government and economic stability in Somalia.

Shipping companies have welcomed the patrols but warned that the area to be protected is vast. EU officials said the mission would coordinate with American, Russian, Indian and other naval forces already operating in the region.
